name: Crowns and bridges

image.caption: How long do crowns and bridges last? This is a common question. Here are some pictuers of a case that is 5 years old. It looks brand new. What a change from before and after. https://t.co/9dZg6ru8L3

lead: Crowns and bridges restore the shape, colour and completeness of teeth. A crown is a cap over a damaged or discoloured tooth, and a bridge fills a gap by anchoring an artificial tooth to neighbouring teeth or implants.

The tooth is shaped, an impression or digital scan is taken, and a restoration in metal, porcelain or zirconia is cemented on, often designed and milled with CAD/CAM systems. They are standard restorative dentistry and are also used cosmetically on teeth that whitening or bonding cannot fix. Typical survival is reported at about 90 to 95 percent over 5 to 10 years.

paras: Treatment takes a couple of visits, with a temporary restoration in between. The finished look is visible once fitted. Restorations typically need replacing after around 10 years.
Preparation permanently removes tooth structure. Reported problems include decay at the margins, porcelain chipping, debonding, gum irritation, wear of opposing teeth and nickel allergy.

angle.text: Crowns restore damaged teeth and bridges fill gaps from missing teeth, so the smile looks complete and uniform. Caps or bridges are fitted over or between teeth, and the restored look is visible once fitted. The methods are long established.

lead: A dental crown is a cap that covers or encircles a tooth or implant to restore its shape, strength and appearance, while a dental bridge is a fixed prosthesis that replaces one or more missing teeth by attaching an artificial tooth (pontic) to neighbouring teeth or implants [1][2].

Crowns are used for badly broken or worn teeth, to strengthen heavily restored teeth, and to improve the look of teeth that simpler cosmetic procedures cannot fix [1]. Common materials include gold and other metal alloys, porcelain-fused-to-metal, all-ceramic and zirconia [1][2].

General references report high medium-term survival for modern restorations, with typical complications including decay at margins, porcelain chipping and debonding [1][2]. Preparing a tooth for a crown involves permanent removal of tooth structure [1].
infobox: Gold, base-metal alloys, porcelain, lithium disilicate, zirconia [1]
CAD/CAM crowns over 95 percent at 5 years; porcelain-fused-to-metal bridges about 95 percent at 10 years [1][2]
Gold crowns and bridges from about 700 BC (Etruscans) [1]

paras: Crowns may be full or partial coverage and are typically made outside the mouth, then cemented. Preparation shapes the tooth to retain the crown while preserving as much structure as possible, after which a temporary crown is fitted [1]. Chairside CAD/CAM systems can design and mill a crown in about 20 minutes without a conventional impression [1]. Reviews describe digital design and manufacturing, including 3D printing, as transforming dental laboratory work [3][4][5].

Zirconia is very hard and strong, requires CAD/CAM milling, and in monolithic form is more opaque, so many dentists avoid it on front teeth. Veneered zirconia looks more natural but the veneering porcelain can chip [1]. Laboratory research has examined the chemical stability and low-temperature ageing of zirconia [6].

Conventional bridges rely on prepared abutment teeth, while resin-bonded (Maryland) bridges use metal wings bonded to etched enamel with minimal preparation [2]. Cantilever designs attach to one side only [2]. A Cochrane review is reported to have found insufficient evidence to favour ceramic over metal-ceramic restorations [2]. Bridges can also be supported by implants [2][7].

CAD/CAM crowns made from certain blocks were reported as over 95 percent clinically successful at five years and at least 90 percent functioning at ten [1]. Porcelain-fused-to-metal bridges are reported at about 95 percent success over ten years, with survival depending on span, position and abutment condition [2]. Cosmetic dentistry summaries put typical bridge lifespan near ten years [8].

For crowns, reported problems include pulp damage from preparation, fracture of root-treated teeth, gum inflammation from poorly placed margins, porcelain chipping, wear of opposing teeth by some materials, and allergy to nickel-containing alloys [1]. For bridges, decay is a common cause of failure, and others are debonding, fracture, plaque accumulation under pontics and colour mismatch [2].
Tooth reduction for crowns and conventional bridges is irreversible, and cosmetic dentistry sources describe some bridge designs as having a reputation for failure [8].

Ceramic materials are chosen mainly for aesthetics compared with all-metal restorations [1]. In cosmetic dentistry, bridges and crowns are listed alongside veneers, bonding, whitening and implants as options for changing the smile [8]. No community material on crowns and bridges was located for this article.

Registered trials include a prospective clinical study of monolithic zirconia restorations and low-temperature degradation in 101 patients [9], an evaluation of ceramic crowns with two cements [10], a clinical study of zirconia bridges [11], a trial of zirconia-reinforced lithium silicate bridges with different cements [12], a study of wear between enamel and veneered versus monolithic zirconia [13], and an implant study in the upper front jaw [14]. Early work on immediate function of implants in the aesthetic zone [7] and on cemented versus screw-retained suprastructures [15] has also been published.
